slides.title: Superpowers: a plugin as the container

elements.text: Superpowers: a plugin as the container
The plugin is the distribution container; skills and hooks supply the behaviour.
Repository: .claude-plugin/plugin.json, hooks/hooks.json with a session-start hook, skills/ and tests/.

SKILL.md has front matter (metadata: name, description) and a body (the procedure)
The brainstorming procedure is seven steps: inspect project, classify scope, clarify requirements, compare approaches, present a design, wait for user approval, invoke writing-plans
The plugin ships the skills, the session-start hook and tests/ together

Type command, async false
Availability is not compliance: the hook guarantees deterministic timing
Runs before the agent acts, and re-runs after clear and compaction
The script reads the bootstrap SKILL.md, escapes the Markdown for JSON and returns it as additionalContext
A SKILL FILE CAN DEFINE SIX COMPONENTS

Hooks intercept requests but cannot rewrite the request to the LLM, so a proxy is required unless you write your own harness. The proxy sits between agent and model provider, while MCP sits beside it, and it applies type-aware compression per content type: logs, code, diffs, JSON, search, HTML/text.
Caveman compresses because context fills up, every turn costs, and compaction loses detail.
The original stays available for retrieval: MCP retrieves it on demand.
The caveat: the skill itself adds input tokens, so whole-session savings are lower than 65%.

Independent tasks, each in an isolated working tree
Buys wall-clock throughput, not answer quality
By hand: one task per session in its own git worktree

A bounded task in fresh context, returning a summary
Buys throughput and focus
Runs alongside the caller and reports back

A larger job carried across many steps
Buys scope
Two ways to keep one running: /goal and /loop

Hand-run parallelism breaks down past a few sessions: you hold the plan, sessions cannot see each other, you reconcile the branches, and it does not repeat because nothing is written down to rerun. Worktrees: ../repo-main (main), ../feat-auth (feature/auth), ../fix-flaky (fix/flaky-test).

slides.title: Subagents: a bounded task in fresh context

elements.text: Subagents: a bounded task in fresh context
A specialized assistant with its own context window, tools and permissions.

Preserve context
Enforce constraints
Reuse anywhere
Parallelize: the slowest subtask sets the total time
Control cost by routing to a cheaper model such as Haiku

Built-ins: Explore, Plan and General-purpose. Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status
A subagent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter whose body becomes the system prompt
Nesting requires Agent in the tools list. Up to 5 levels are allowed, 2 to 3 the sweet spot

slides.title: Subagents and agent teams are not the same

elements.text: Subagents and agent teams are not the same

An agent team is several Claude Code sessions working together: one lead, several teammates, a shared task list, and a mailbox (a JSON inbox per agent). Use cases: review, independent modules, debugging and cross-layer work. Teams are experimental and off by default: they cost more tokens and are worth it only when the work needs discussion.
This is a coordination-cost decision, not a capability decision.
Runs until a verifiable end state holds. It stops when the end state is met, or when --max-tries runs out.
/goal "npm run lint exits with zero errors"
Re-runs a prompt on a schedule until you stop it. The default prompt lives in .claude/loop.md; press Esc to end.
A JavaScript script orchestrating many subagents in the background, entered by typing "ultracode" or running /effort ultracode.

slides.title: The 16-agent C compiler: scale and limits

elements.text: The 16-agent C compiler: scale and limits
About 100,000 lines of code. Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM and RISC-V. QEMU, FFmpeg, Postgres, Redis, Doom. Roughly 99% pass rate on major test suites.

Merge conflicts were frequent
Parallelism stopped helping on a shared kernel failure
It still leaned on GCC for part of the 16-bit x86 work
The generated code was less efficient than GCC output

Programming 1.0 is programming hardware, 2.0 is programming a language, 3.0 is expressing the goal. It trades higher productivity for more uncertainty. The term is the lecturer's, explicitly different from Andrej Karpathy's definition; Software 3.0 is his: human language and context, then LLM, then action.

State assumptions up front
Have the model confirm anything ambiguous before it executes

Separate proposal from execution
Manage context explicitly: own memory, provenance and retrieval, and expire stale information
Specify outcomes, not prompts

Tighten the generate-verify loop
Measure one level deeper
"Do not expect the agent to be deterministic; make the surrounding system dependable." And: "match autonomy to risk: the more autonomy the higher uncertainty and risk."

slides.title: Three things to carry out of Lecture 3

elements.text: Three things to carry out of Lecture 3
The same model and tools behave differently under different instructions. The instructions are the design surface.
Scale has three independent axes - breadth, focus, duration - and each multi-agent mechanism buys a different one at a different cost.
Compression and coordination are architectural decisions (proxy, hooks, MCP, worktrees, task lists), not configuration. Do not expect the agent to be deterministic, so match autonomy to risk.
